summary.text: The Hadley cell is a global-scale tropical circulation in which air rises near the equator, flows poleward high up, sinks around 30 degrees latitude and returns near the surface.
Its surface branch shows up as the trade winds, which gather air and moisture into the tropical zone where Earth's heaviest rains fall.
Its sinking branches suppress rainfall, and many of Earth's deserts lie in the subtropics where that air comes down.

facts.label: Named after
facts.value: George Hadley, who proposed it in 1735

facts.label: Recent change
facts.value: Expanded poleward since at least the 1980s

items.prompt: Many of the world's deserts sit near 30 degrees latitude. How does the Hadley cell help explain this?

options.label: Air rises there and drops its rain
Air sinks there and suppresses rain
Trade winds blow the rain out to sea
Upper winds heat the ground below

items.explain: The sinking branches of the Hadley cells suppress rainfall, and many deserts line up with where that air descends.

items.prompt: What fundamentally sets the Hadley circulation in motion?
items.explain: It is a thermally direct circulation that arises from differences in heating between the tropics and the subtropics.

items.prompt: In July, during northern summer, which side of the globe has most of the Hadley circulation's rising air?
items.explain: In summer and winter a single cross-equatorial cell dominates, with air rising in the summer hemisphere and sinking in the winter one.

items.prompt: As the seasons change, the rainy belt where the trade winds converge shifts north and south. What does this shifting cause?
items.explain: Shifts in the Intertropical Convergence Zone tied to the Hadley circulation's seasonal changes cause monsoons.

items.prompt: Why do the trade winds blow partly westward instead of straight toward the equator?

options.label: The Sun's daily path pulls them

items.explain: The Coriolis force deflects the trade winds, so they blow partly westward in both hemispheres.

items.prompt: Roughly how much of Earth's surface area lies under the Hadley circulation?
items.explain: It spans roughly from the Tropic of Cancer to the Tropic of Capricorn, covering almost half of Earth's surface.

paragraphs.heading: A loop of tropical air
paragraphs.text: The Hadley cell, or Hadley circulation, is a vast loop of air over the tropics. Air rises near the equator, travels toward the poles near the tropopause some 12–15 km up, cools and sinks in the subtropics around 30 degrees latitude, then flows back toward the equator near the ground. Averaged over a year, there is one such cell on each side of the equator. Together they span roughly from the Tropic of Cancer to the Tropic of Capricorn, almost half of Earth's surface, and fill the whole depth of the troposphere.

paragraphs.heading: Why it exists
paragraphs.text: The loop is driven by uneven heating of Earth's surface. Over a year, the equatorial regions take in more of the Sun's radiation than they give off, while higher latitudes give off more than they receive. With nothing to move heat between them, the equator would keep warming and the higher latitudes keep cooling. Air rising in some places and sinking in others sets up a pressure gradient force, which powers the Hadley circulation and spreads heat, keeping the planet in balance over the long run.

paragraphs.heading: How the loop is pushed
paragraphs.text: Near the surface, warm air rising at the equator and air sinking in the subtropics leave lower pressure at the equator and higher pressure in the subtropics, and that difference drives surface air toward the equator. Higher up, heat released as water vapour condenses in the tropics keeps the pressure aloft higher there than in the subtropics at the same height. This upper difference is the stronger of the two, and it pushes the high-level air toward the poles. Because the air comes back to where it began and heating controls it so strongly, the cell is a closed, thermally driven loop.

paragraphs.heading: Trade winds and the rain belt
paragraphs.text: The lower branch of the cell is the trade winds, which carry air toward the equator in both hemispheres. The Coriolis force turns them so they blow partly westward rather than straight toward the equator. Crossing the tropical oceans, they gather moisture from evaporation. Where they converge, in the Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ), the moist air is forced upward, and this belt holds Earth's heaviest rains. Seasonal shifts of the ITCZ bring the monsoons.

paragraphs.heading: Deserts and seasons
paragraphs.text: Where the cell's air sinks, it builds subtropical ridges over the oceans and holds back rain. Many of the world's deserts and dry lands lie in the subtropics, right under these sinking branches. In the summer and winter months the pattern changes: one cell stretches across the equator, with air going up in the summer hemisphere and coming down in the winter one. On average the southern cell is slightly stronger and reaches a little way into the Northern Hemisphere.

paragraphs.heading: Discovery and a changing climate
paragraphs.text: The circulation is named after George Hadley, who in 1735 explained the trade winds by proposing cells as wide as a hemisphere, powered by uneven heating. Proof of a broad circulation like his came in the mid-20th century, once radiosondes made routine observations of the upper troposphere possible. Observations and climate models show the cell has spread toward the poles since at least the 1980s because of climate change, and models project it will widen and weaken through the 21st century. Similar circulations may also exist on Venus and Mars.
